guide.summary: Use Linear OAuth2 with the read scope only, so each connected customer account can read issue titles through the GraphQL API with cursor pagination. Create the OAuth application in a dedicated workspace, test with your own test account, and avoid write scopes. Customer-facing review and distribution requirements are not established by the supplied sources and must be verified before rollout.

findings.title: OAuth2 is documented for third-party integrations
findings.detail: Linear documents OAuth2 as the recommended method for applications that integrate with Linear and for applications used by others.

evidence.quote: Linear supports OAuth2 authentication, which is recommended if you’re building applications to integrate with Linear.

findings.title: Request the read scope for issue title reads
findings.detail: The read scope is the default and gives read access to the authorized user's account, which covers the GraphQL issue title query.

evidence.quote: * `read` - (Default) Read access for the user's account. This scope will always be present.
--data '{ "query": "{ issues { nodes { id title } } }" }' \

findings.title: Do not request write, issue-write or admin scopes
findings.detail: issues:create covers creating and updating issues, write is broader than needed, and admin should never be requested without absolute need. These conflict with the read-only boundary.

evidence.quote: * `write` - Write access for the user's account. If your application only needs to create comments, use a more targeted scope
* `issues:create` - Allows creating and updating issues, and creating their attachments
* `admin` - Full access to admin level endpoints. You should never ask for this permission unless it's absolutely needed

findings.title: Create the OAuth application in a dedicated workspace
findings.detail: Linear recommends a dedicated workspace for managing the OAuth2 application because every admin user in that workspace gets access to it.

evidence.quote: > [!NOTE] > It is **highly recommended** you create a workspace for the purpose of managing the OAuth2 Application, as each admin user will have access.

findings.title: Use pagination arguments for complete title lists
findings.detail: Issue lists return paginated results using first and after with pageInfo.endCursor and hasNextPage, so the client must follow cursors until hasNextPage is false.

evidence.quote: issues(first: 10) { edges {
} ``` To query the next 10, simply pass the value of `pageInfo.endCursor` as `after` parameter for the next request. You can do this as long as `pageInfo.hasNextPage` return true

steps.detail: Register the Linear OAuth2 application in a workspace reserved for managing it. Record the client ID, client secret and redirect URI.
steps.doneWhen: The OAuth application exists with a redirect URI and a stored client ID and client secret.

steps.title: Implement the authorization request and callback for scope read
steps.detail: Build the authorize request with response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope=read and a random state value. Store the code exchange result for the connected account.
steps.doneWhen: The authorize URL contains scope=read and state, and the callback can receive the authorization code.

evidence.quote: ### Example ```http GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL&state=SECURE_RANDOM&scope=read HTTP/1.1
`state` | (optional, **recommended**) Prevents CSRF attacks and should always be supplied. Read more about it here.
* `read` - (Default) Read access for the user's account. This scope will always be present.

steps.title: Authorize your own test workspace account and exchange the code
steps.detail: Sign in with a test account in your own test workspace, approve the read scope, then exchange the returned code for a Bearer access token. Expected response includes token_type Bearer and expires_in.
steps.doneWhen: The test account returns a Bearer access token with read access.

evidence.quote: "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 86399,
### Example ```http GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL&state=SECURE_RANDOM&scope=read HTTP/1.1

steps.title: Read the first page of issue titles
steps.detail: Call the GraphQL endpoint with the Bearer token to read the first issue titles. Expected response: data.issues.nodes with id and title, plus pageInfo with hasNextPage and endCursor. Boundary check: confirm the granted access is read only and the outgoing request contains only the query above, with no mutation.
steps.doneWhen: The response returns issue titles and pageInfo, and the request log shows only the query.

evidence.quote: --data '{ "query": "{ issues { nodes { id title } } }" }' \
} ``` To query the next 10, simply pass the value of `pageInfo.endCursor` as `after` parameter for the next request. You can do this as long as `pageInfo.hasNextPage` return true

request.example: curl '-X' 'POST' 'https://api.linear.app/graphql' '-H' 'Content-Type: application/json' '-H' 'Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>' '--data' '{"query":"{ issues(first: 10) { nodes { id title } pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } } }"}'

fields: Access token: backend OAuth exchange for the test account; keep it out of this guide

steps.title: Read the next page of issue titles using the cursor
steps.detail: Pass pageInfo.endCursor from the first response as the after argument. Expected response: the next set of issue titles and updated pageInfo. Boundary check: confirm via the request log that the test sends only read queries and that the token has no write scope, without attempting any create, update or delete.
steps.doneWhen: The second page returns different titles and the pagination cursor is confirmed, with only query requests in the log.
